crash.title: The Panic of 1873
crash.line: A railway and property boom burst on the Vienna stock exchange, spread to New York, and opened a long worldwide slump.

crash.title: Black Monday
crash.line: After a five-year bull market, the Dow fell 22.6% on 19 October 1987, its worst day ever, as markets crashed worldwide.

crash.title: The dot-com bubble bursts
crash.line: Investors poured money into internet startups until the Nasdaq peaked in March 2000, then it lost about 78% over two years.

tariffs.title: Colbert's tariff war on the Dutch
tariffs.line: France's minister Colbert put steep duties on Dutch goods, the Dutch banned French wares, and the trade war fed France's 1672 invasion.

tariffs.title: The Chicken War
tariffs.line: When Europe's Common Market taxed cheap American chicken, the US hit back with a 25% tariff on light trucks that still stands.

tariffs.title: The US–China trade war
tariffs.line: The US taxed steel, aluminum and hundreds of billions in Chinese imports, and China hit back with tariffs on American farm goods.

bankrun.title: The Overend, Gurney collapse
bankrun.line: London's biggest discount bank failed, crowds besieged banks on “Black Friday”, and the Bank of England lent freely to stop the panic.

bankrun.title: Argentina freezes bank accounts
bankrun.line: As savers drained Argentina's banks, the government capped cash withdrawals in December 2001, sparking riots and a debt default.

bankrun.title: The run on Northern Rock
bankrun.line: Savers queued outside Northern Rock branches after it sought emergency Bank of England help, Britain's first bank run in over a century.

dust.title: The Laki haze over Europe
dust.line: Iceland's Laki eruption spread a sulfurous haze across Europe, and about a fifth of Icelanders died in the famine that followed.

dust.title: London's Great Smog
dust.line: Coal smoke and fog blacked out London for five days, killing thousands and pushing Parliament to pass the 1956 Clean Air Act.

dust.title: San Francisco's orange sky
dust.line: Smoke from record wildfires amid heat and drought turned San Francisco's sky dark orange, with streetlights on at midday.

munich.title: D'Annunzio seizes Fiume
munich.line: Poet Gabriele D'Annunzio led armed volunteers into the Adriatic port, claiming it for its Italian majority; Italy annexed it in 1924.

munich.title: Turkish troops land in Cyprus
munich.line: After a Greek-backed coup, Turkey sent troops, saying it was protecting Turkish Cypriots, and took about a third of the island.

munich.title: The Russia–Georgia war
munich.line: Russia fought Georgia over South Ossetia, saying it was defending residents holding Russian passports, then recognized two breakaway regions as independent.

martians.title: Mary Toft's rabbit births
martians.line: An English servant claimed to give birth to rabbits, and even a royal surgeon believed her until she confessed to the hoax.

martians.title: The Cottingley Fairies
martians.line: Two English girls photographed paper cutout fairies, and Sherlock Holmes author Arthur Conan Doyle championed the pictures as real.

martians.title: The BBC's spaghetti harvest
martians.line: A straight-faced BBC report showed Swiss farmers picking spaghetti from trees on April Fools' Day, and viewers asked how to grow it.

martians.title: The Hitler Diaries
martians.line: German magazine Stern paid millions for diaries said to be Hitler's, and within two weeks experts exposed them as modern forgeries.

einstein.title: Atomic scientists start the Doomsday Clock
einstein.line: Manhattan Project scientists launched the Doomsday Clock, set at seven minutes to midnight, to warn the world about nuclear war.

einstein.title: The Asilomar gene-splicing conference
einstein.line: Biologists who had just invented gene splicing paused their own experiments and met at Asilomar, California, to draft safety rules.

einstein.title: Gene editors call for a pause
einstein.line: CRISPR pioneer Jennifer Doudna urged a pause on editing human embryos, and a Washington summit called heritable edits irresponsible for now.

transistor.title: Faraday turns magnetism into electricity
transistor.line: Michael Faraday showed in his London lab that moving magnets make electric current, the principle behind every power station generator.

transistor.title: Haber pulls fertilizer from the air
transistor.line: Fritz Haber made ammonia from air on a tabletop machine; scaled up as Haber-Bosch, its fertilizer now helps feed billions.

transistor.title: Fleming discovers penicillin
transistor.line: Alexander Fleming noticed mold killing bacteria in a London lab dish, and mass-produced penicillin later launched the antibiotic age.

transistor.title: Berners-Lee invents the Web
transistor.line: At CERN, Tim Berners-Lee proposed a system of linked documents, and the World Wide Web he built now connects billions.

mccarthy.title: The trial of Galileo
mccarthy.line: The Inquisition convicted Galileo for teaching that Earth circles the Sun, banned his book and kept him under house arrest for life.

mccarthy.title: The first Red Scare raids
mccarthy.line: In the first Red Scare, federal raids rounded up thousands of suspected radicals for their politics and deported hundreds, including Emma Goldman.

mccarthy.title: The Dixie Chicks boycott
mccarthy.line: After singer Natalie Maines criticized President George W. Bush before the Iraq War, country radio stations across America stopped playing the band.

suez.title: The Suez Canal closes for eight years
suez.line: The Six-Day War closed the Suez Canal until 1975, trapping a fleet of cargo ships and sending tankers around Africa.

suez.title: The Ever Given blocks Suez
suez.line: The giant container ship Ever Given wedged across the Suez Canal for six days, and some ships detoured around Africa instead.

sputnik.title: The Soviets test an atomic bomb
sputnik.line: The Soviet Union tested its first atomic bomb years before US experts expected, and Truman ordered a crash hydrogen bomb program.

sputnik.title: Japan's chip lead alarms America
sputnik.line: Japanese firms had overtaken America in memory chips, so Washington backed the new SEMATECH consortium with federal money to catch up.
